historyNotes.text: Property offenses account for 57,084 of the 70,003 reports at Boston’s 1989 peak.
The Web is announced publicly. August 1991 · cultural landmark
historyNotes.editorialReason: Familiar cultural milestone; temporal orientation, not a crime-cause claim.

historyNotes.text: The decline was already underway: 55,555 reports in 1993, 21% below 1989.
Operation Ceasefire began in 1996, targeting youth firearm violence.
historyNotes.editorialReason: Local violence-prevention initiative directly relevant to the topic; distinguish its narrow target from all crime.

historyNotes.text: By 2000, reported property crime was about half its 1989 level.
2003 · The Big Dig brings the Central Artery underground through downtown Boston.
historyNotes.editorialReason: A visible transformation of Boston’s geography locates this era; no crime-effect claim.

historyNotes.text: The first YouTube upload. April 2005 · cultural landmark
historyNotes.editorialReason: Familiar cultural milestone; temporal orientation, not a crime-cause claim.

historyNotes.text: By 2010, violent index offenses numbered 5,819—55% below their 1989 count.
The FBI series ends at 20,110 reports—71% below the 1989 peak.
March 2020: Boston’s public-health emergency begins during the COVID-19 pandemic.
historyNotes.editorialReason: Local emergency marks the pandemic disruption; the chart does not establish its causal effect.

historyNotes.text: After the 2022 low of 27,537, the annual count rose to 31,239 in 2023.

annotations.text: The map shows a sample of published locations; district totals include reports without coordinates.
2022 ends with 27,537 crime-classified reports—the lowest complete year since 2016.
D4 / South End recorded 5,022 reports in 2023, up from 4,156 in 2022.
August 2024: 2,944 crime-classified reports, the highest month in this five-year window.
Property offenses account for 18,186 of the 29,963 crime-classified reports in 2025.
The annual total fell 36% from 2016 to 2025. The map shows how unevenly reports are distributed.
